title: A Giant Leap: AI and healthcare
text:
Just read Robert Wachter's A Giant Leap, an accessible, well-written, and clinically grounded primer — arguably the best single-volume introduction to AI in healthcare available today. Wachter, an academic hospitalist chair of medicine at UCSF, is a serious thinker, not a naive booster, and his awareness of past digital disappointments (his previous book, The Digital Doctor, was a warning about EHRs) gives his cautious optimism some credibility.
But the book ultimately reflects the view from the top of American academic medicine — optimistic, well-funded, and influential, but not representative of where most care actually happens. Readers should treat it as an essential starting point, not a verdict.

I found the book to be a refreshing read documenting the many failed attempts at "AI in healthcare" spanning many decades where the initial failed attempts were overly ambitious (i.e. focusing on the most complex tasks such as diagnosis and interpretation). He reviews the gradual transition from paper charts to electronic medical records (EHR) in the early 2000s, with the unintended consequence of tasking clinicians with manually typing out their daily notes (keeping them glued to the screen) and frustrating them with administrative burden including managing an in box from patients and fighting insurers for prior authorization requests. The book thankfully transitions to the past 5 years with the introduction of generative AI, being rapidly applied to some of these basic tasks (i.e. new software that captures a routine doctor-patient visit into a standard chart note referred to as "AI scribe" or "ambient AI"), far exceeding all prior attempts (i.e. dictation transcription, human scribes, templates). Generative AI is being used to summarize large patient volumes with great accuracy. In addition, he notes niche applications where AI is starting to process large volumes of data to provide innovative applications (i.e. take a standard EKG and accurately provide a cardiac ejection fraction!).

Wachter does a great job introducing (name dropping?) a variety of startups fiercely competing in this AI healthcare scribe space (Abridge, Epic-MS partnership, Oracle/Cerner), or the prior auth space (Ochsner Health opening its EHR to an insurer, or Elevance/Anthem connecting with Montefiore's Epic EHR). He gushes over the concept of a doctor "digital twin" being embraced at the Mayo Clinic or the AI medical student application screening tool being used at NYU Langone! 

One highly interesting section discussed the inability of large private companies to crack the primary care model in the US. These include failures at Amazon's One Medical, CVS's Oak Street Health, Walgreen's VillageMD, and start-ups Google's Forward, UK's Babylon Health, and now Cure Ai. The bet is whether private tech enterprise will figure it out or much more likely established health systems will dominate and integrate AI.

Critical Weaknesses

1. Optimism bias is structural, not incidental.

Wachter's position — an elite academic physician at a flagship institution with deep ties to the tech-medicine world — shapes his perspective in ways the book does not fully interrogate. His 100+ interviews are largely with "pioneers," which almost by definition skews toward boosters. Skeptics, frontline nurses, community health workers, and underserved patients are not the architects of his narrative.

2. The "better than broken" standard is dangerously low.
His central argument — AI just needs to beat a dysfunctional status quo — could be used to justify deploying undertested tools on vulnerable populations. A system causing a million annual harms is not a neutral baseline. This framing risks accelerating AI adoption before rigorous outcome data exists across diverse patient populations.

3. Algorithmic risks are acknowledged but not sufficiently weighted.
Wachter acknowledges algorithmic drift — where AI performance degrades over time as science, policies, or patient populations change — but treats it as a manageable concern rather than a systemic risk. The structural conditions under which AI fails (in under-resourced hospitals, in populations underrepresented in training data) receive far less attention than its successes at elite institutions. 

4. The equity problem is underexplored.
The book largely reflects the experience of well-resourced health systems. The AI tools Wachter describes are, for now, predominantly being piloted at places like UCSF and Mayo Clinic. What happens when stripped-down versions reach safety-net hospitals or rural clinics is largely unaddressed — a major gap given that healthcare inequality is arguably the system's deepest failure.

5. It risks aging poorly, fast.
The book's insertion of AI into healthcare is set against a backdrop of eroding trust between patients and clinicians, and a political landscape where partisanship has infected patients' perceptions of clinical recommendations — dynamics Wachter notes but doesn't fully integrate into his optimistic arc. In a field moving as fast as this one, a framework built in 2025â2026 may need significant revision within 2â3 years. 

6. The blurb problem.
The endorsements — from Marc Benioff (Salesforce CEO), Vinod Khosla (AI investor), and Microsoft Research's president — signal that this book is embedded in the same tech-medicine industrial complex it is meant to evaluate. These aren't neutral validators.

I highly recommend this book to anyone in healthcare and anyone who has interest in how AI is changing our world.

Key Reference:

Screening for Cardiac Contractile Dysfunction Using an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Electrocardiogram.
Nature Medicine. 2019. Attia ZI, Kapa S, Lopez-Jimenez F, et al.
